label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
Here's a draft. Fix any details I've gotten wrong, since I only know what you told me.

---

**Why I'm not dropping the busing project (Jess, this one's mostly for you)**

Jess texted me last night. Paraphrasing only a little: *it's one assignment, don't torch your job over it.* By this morning, about half the group chat had piled on in agreement. I'm not mad. She's a friend who's looking out for me and she said what a good friend would say. But I didn't want to answer fifteen texts one at a time from my phone while pretending to grade, so I'm doing it here, once, and then I'll leave it alone.

Quick background for everyone who doesn't live inside my head. I teach US History II at Cobb Street High, juniors, two sections. For the last four years, one of the projects has been this: each kid interviews someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston in 1974 to 1976, the busing and desegregation years. Ten minutes of recording, plus a two-page reflection. That's the whole assignment. I've never had a complaint about it until now.

The complaint came as an email to Dr. Halvorsen, with a school committee member cc'd. It said the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." Halvorsen would very much like me to quietly drop it, and I think she'd like it to happen before anyone has to sit in a room about it. There is a room, though. Thursday, Nov 19, 3:15, me and Halvorsen and the parent.

Here's the part where Jess is right, and I want to say so plainly. I could get burned. I've had tenure since 2021, which people assume makes me bulletproof, and it doesn't. Halvorsen still builds my schedule. She still decides who gets AP. Nobody has to fire me to make my life a lot more annoying for a lot of years. Jess left teaching in 2019 and she remembers how that works. She's not being cynical, she's being accurate.

And I'm scared, a little. I'd love to tell you I'm calm and principled about this, but I'm not brave about it. I've reread that email more times than I'd like to admit. I'm doing this anyway, and I think that's the more honest way to put it.

So why.

In 2023, a kid I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. She drove a school bus in Southie in 1974. She had never told anyone in the family about it. Not his mom, not anybody. He sat down with a recorder, asked her what she remembered, and she told him. He played about forty seconds of it for the class. When it ended nobody said a word for what felt like a full minute. I've taught for a long time and I can count on one hand the times a room of sixteen-year-olds has been quiet because they wanted to be and not because I made them.

That's what the project can do. A kid goes looking for a grandparent and finds a person who was *there*, who had a bus window and a street and a fear that is nowhere in a textbook.

And the textbook, by the way, gives all of this one paragraph. One. This is the history of the city these kids live in. Some of them live on streets where it happened. They walk past the buildings. And the official version they're handed fits in a paragraph you can skim between bells.

Last year a girl in my class found out her uncle was one of the people throwing rocks at the buses. She was upset about it, really upset. We talked after class twice. I didn't try to fix it, because I don't think it's fixable and I don't think it should be. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year. It wasn't the best because it was tidy. It was the best because she wasn't pretending anymore that the past was somewhere else, belonging to other people. It was in her family, at the dinner table, in a person she loved. She had to sit with that, and she wrote about sitting with it better than most adults I know could.

That's the part I can't un-know. The parent's email says the project reopens wounds. Sometimes it does. The wounds were already there. What the project does is hand a kid a flashlight and a recorder, and a reason to ask.

Now here's the part I want to be fair about, because I do think the parent has a point. The word "pressure" in that email stuck with me, and I don't think it's nothing. Asking a fifteen- or sixteen-year-old to sit across from their grandfather and ask about the worst thing he ever did, or watched, or failed to stop, with a grade attached, is a real ask. Some families can hold that. Some can't, or not yet, or not on a school deadline. I've framed the project as an invitation for four years, but a graded assignment is a graded assignment, and a kid can feel the difference between "you could" and "you'd better."

So I'm not going into Thursday to fight her. I'm going in to tell her she's right about something, and that I want to fix it.

Here's the plan. The project stays, and I'm adding an alternate option so that no kid has to interview family. They can interview a librarian or an archivist, someone who works with this history from the outside. Or they can use the recorded interviews from past years, with permission from the kids and families who made them. Same recording length, same reflection, same grade. Nobody has to sit across from a relative and ask the hard question unless they choose to.

That's the line for me, and I've thought about where it goes. The kids who feel most uncomfortable with this are very often the ones who'd get the most out of it. I really believe that. But I don't get to force anyone. Believing something is good for a kid doesn't give me the right to make a kid do it, especially to someone they love. Take away the pressure and what's left is an offer, and I'm comfortable defending an offer.

Jess, I think this is where we might actually be closer than the texts made it sound. You said don't torch your job over one assignment. And if the assignment were just an assignment, I'd agree with you. If a parent complained about a worksheet, I'd swap the worksheet. I've done it. I don't dig in over things like that.

But I can't make myself see this one as one assignment. It's the one thing I do all year where I feel like I'm doing the actual job. If I quietly drop it, then what I'd be saying, to Halvorsen and to myself, is that it was something to be a little embarrassed about, a thing I did that needed to be tucked away. And I don't think that. I'd know I didn't think that, and I'd be teaching with that for the next however many years.

I'm not asking you to agree. I'd honestly just like you to know why, so when I'm sitting there Thursday you're not wondering if I've lost my mind. I might lose. Halvorsen might say the alternate option isn't enough, or the committee member might get involved, and I might end up with a smaller version of the project than I want, or a bad year. I've made peace with some of that. Not all of it. Some.

To everyone else in the group chat who weighed in: thanks, truly. I know you were all being kind. I'm okay. Scared, but okay.

Jess, I'll text you Thursday after the meeting, whatever happens. You'll be the first one I tell. And you can say "told you so" if it goes badly. I'll even let you.

---

One thing to think about before you post: the draft names Halvorsen, your school, and the exact meeting time. Even on a small blog, that's easy to find and screenshot, and it ties your name to an active personnel-adjacent matter before Thursday. You might swap in "my principal" and "my school" and cut the date, which costs nothing in the post. I can make that change if you want.
